targets.title: Object individuation in infancy: the use of featural information in reasoning about occlusion events
targets.evidence_quote:
We report a replication experiment of a mechanized version of the seminal wide-screen/narrow-screen design of Wilcox and
           Baillargeon (1998) with 9.5-month-old infants (𝑁 = 80).
targets.outcome_quote:
Across conditions with three different screen sizes, the results from both
           methodologies revealed a clear and interesting pattern: the looking times increased as a significantly linear function of reduced
           screen sizes, that is, independently of the number of different objects involved. There was no indication in the data that the infants
           made use of the featural differences between the different-looking objects involved.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The discussion explicitly states that the results partly replicate the original: longer narrow-screen looking replicates, but the discrimination assumption is unsupported. This overall partial-replication verdict governs despite the alternative theoretical interpretation. The abstract quote preserves the literal full-width text; the discussion verdict is interrupted by the other column in the supplied extraction.

reasoning: New infant data retest the 9.5-month wide/narrow-screen experiment [4, Experiment 3], and the added direct narrow-control comparison retests the ball-ball/ball-box finding of [5]. The adult forced-choice task is new. Other papers describe background, interpretations, or prior experiments rather than independently designated retests here; the smaller-object control is explicitly not replicated. No original-data reanalysis is reported. Reference [23] is only an ancillary see-also citation without a separately specified retested finding.
